Evidence for the cards that pass:
- 01: "By default, a pod is non-isolated for ingress; all inbound connections are allowed."
- 03: "the ingress rules for each are combined additively"
- 04: "both the egress policy on the source pod and the ingress policy on the destination pod need to allow the connection"
- 05: "An empty selector matches all pods in the policy's namespace." (also on the declare-network-policy page)
- 06: "policies that contain an egress section are assumed to affect egress, and all policies (whether or not they contain an ingress section) are assumed to affect ingress"
- 09: endPort "cannot be defined if ... the port field is defined as a named (string) port". API server validation rejects it, as the card's explanation says.

One gap in coverage: the scope lists "a default-deny egress policy also blocks DNS unless DNS is allowed", and no card tests it. The concept page has a Caution box that says so. If the deck owner wants it, it would be a TRUE card, so it should replace a true card (07 is the weakest) rather than 02 or 08.

Minor style note: five statements open with "With a plugin enforcing NetworkPolicy" (or a variant of it), and the opener appears in both true and false cards, so it is not a tell. Card 01's "incoming TCP traffic" narrows the statement for no reason, but it is not wrong.

- 02: the Service page says \"A Service can map any incoming port to a targetPort\". The debug-service page says \"These commands use the Pod port (9376), rather than the Service port (80).\"
- 03: the Service page says \"This works even if there is a mixture of Pods in the Service using a single configured name, with the same network protocol available via different port numbers.\"
- 05: dns-pod-service says headless Services resolve \"to the set of IPs of all of the Pods selected by the Service\" and that \"the Pod needs to be ready in order to have a record unless publishNotReadyAddresses=True\". \"By default\" covers publishNotReadyAddresses.
- 06: dns-pod-service says \"DNS queries that don't specify a namespace are limited to the Pod's namespace.\"

Actions such as kubectl port-forward service/<service-name> ... where the service has no selector will fail due to this constraint.\" A caveat that does not change the answer: in practice kubectl already fails on the client side, because it resolves a Pod from the Service selector. The section never tests some items its scope lists: nodePort, kubectl expose, Service environment variables needing the Service to exist before the Pod, and the debug-service troubleshooting steps. - 06: "/foo/bar ... does not match /foo/barbaz", and the table row "/aaa/bbbxyz No".

- 09: "defaultBackend is the backend that should handle requests that don't match any rule."

Card 07 (ImplementationSpecific with Kubernetes-defined regex, False) is borderline. Its false reason is only the qualifier "defined by Kubernetes", while some controllers do offer regex under ImplementationSpecific. I let it pass. A cleaner false version would be: "With pathType ImplementationSpecific, Kubernetes applies Prefix matching to the path." The source says "matching is up to the IngressClass".

The scope topics "Ingress exposes only HTTP and HTTPS" and "the Ingress API is GA and frozen; the Kubernetes project recommends Gateway" are not covered. That is acceptable, but one of the replacements could cover them instead.

duplicates.why: Both test the opt-in flags of the Kustomize labels field: by default labels go only to metadata, and includeSelectors/includeTemplates switch on selectors and Pod templates. 2.3-10's statement ('with includeTemplates true and includeSelectors false') shows that selectors are opt-in, which answers 2.3-09. These are two sides of one distinction. Keep 2.3-09, the more consequential selector fact.

Both rest on one fact: kubectl port-forward to a Service resolves to a single backing Pod and does not use Service routing. Once you know 5.2-08 ('selects one matching Pod'), 5.2-10 follows, because external addresses are not Pods. 5.2-10's mechanism ('API server blocks proxying to endpoints that do not map to Pods') is also shaky: kubectl itself refuses a Service without a selector.
